{"id": "96482ddd-d0b1-423b-837d-f92b299383a0", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_IFFNZwHs55jndqh9HJND6O", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters\",\"context\":\"# Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails helps detect sensitive information, such as personally identifiable information\\n(PII), in input prompts or model responses using sensitive information filters. This filter is a probabilistic machine learning (ML) based solution that is context-dependent\\nand detects sensitive information based on the context within input prompts or model responses. You can configure by selecting from a set of built-in PIIs offered by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails specific to your use case\\nor organization by defining it along with regular expressions (custom regex) that work based on pattern matching to block or mask PII data.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nThis filter evaluates text content only. In tool use (function calling) workloads, it does not evaluate the following, so PII in these fields is neither blocked nor masked:\\n\\n* PII the model generates into tool call arguments (`toolUse.input` in Converse, `tool_use` parameters in InvokeModel). For example, if the model passes a customer's email address to a tool that writes a file, that address is not masked.\\n* PII in tool results your application returns to the model (`toolResult`).\\n* PII in the tool definitions you supply (`toolSpec.description`, `toolSpec.inputSchema`).\\n\\nSensitive information detection works across both natural language and code domains,\\nincluding code syntax, comments, string literals, and hybrid content. This helps\\nidentify PII embedded in code elements such as variable names, hardcoded credentials, or\\ncode documentation.\\n\\nYou can configure the following modes for handling sensitive information that\\nguardrails detects:\\n\\n* **Block** \u2014 Sensitive information filter\\n policies can block requests or responses that include sensitive information.\\n Examples of such applications might include general questions and answers\\n based on public documents. If sensitive information is detected in\\n the prompt or response, the guardrail blocks all the content and returns a\\n message that you configure.\\n* **Mask** \u2014 Sensitive information filter\\n policies can anonymize or redact information from model requests or responses.\\n For example, guardrails mask PIIs while generating summaries of conversations\\n between users and customer service agents. If sensitive information is detected\\n in the model request or response, the guardrail masks it and replaces it with\\n the PII type (for example, `{NAME}` or `{EMAIL}`).\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails offers the following PIIs to block or anonymize:\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-sensitive-filters.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Create your guardrail\",\"context\":\"# Create your guardrail\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails offers filters that you can configure to\\nhelp avoid undesirable and harmful content and remove or mask sensitive information for\\nprivacy protection.\\n\\nYou can configure the following filters with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails:\\n\\n* **Content filters** \u2014 This filter helps you detect and filter harmful\\n text or image content in input prompts or model responses (excluding reasoning content). Filtering is done based\\n on detection of certain predefined harmful content categories: Hate, Insults,\\n Sexual, Violence, Misconduct and Prompt Attack. You can configure the filter\\n strength for each of these categories based on your use cases. With Standard tier, detection of undesirable content is extended to protect against harmful content within code elements including\\n comments, variable and function names, and string literals.\\n* **Prompt attacks** \u2014 Offered as a category within content filters, this filter can help you detect and\\n filter prompt attacks including jailbreaks, prompt injections, and prompt leakages (Standard tier only). This capability helps you detect prompts that are intended\\n to bypass content moderation, override instructions, or generate harmful content.\\n* **Denied topics** \u2014 You can define a set of\\n topics to avoid within your generative AI application. For example, a banking\\n assistant application can be designed to help avoid topics related to illegal\\n investment advice. With Standard tier,\\n content filters extend to code domains.\\n* **Word filters** \u2014 You can define a set of\\n custom words or phrases (exact match) that you want to detect and block in the\\n interaction between your users and generative AI applications. For example, you can\\n detect and block profanity (using a ready-to-use option) as well as specific custom words such as competitor\\n names, or other offensive words.\\n* **Sensitive information filters** \u2014 Can help\\n you detect sensitive content such as Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in\\n standard formats or custom regex entities in user inputs and FM responses. This filter is a probabilistic maching learning (ML)\\n based solution that is context dependent. It detects sensitive information based on the context within input prompts or model responses. Based on\\n your use case, you can block or mask inputs and responses containing sensitive information. For example, you can redact users' personal information while\\n generating summaries from customer and agent conversation transcripts.\\n* **Contextual grounding checks** \u2014 Can\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"CreateGuardrail\",\"context\":\"# CreateGuardrail\\n\\nCreates a guardrail to detect and filter harmful content in your generative AI\\napplication.\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails provides the following safeguards (also known as policies) to detect and filter harmful\\ncontent:\\n\\n* **Content filters** - Detect and filter harmful\\n text or image content in input prompts or model responses. Filtering is done based\\n on detection of certain predefined harmful content categories: Hate, Insults,\\n Sexual, Violence, Misconduct and Prompt Attack. You also can adjust the filter\\n strength for each of these categories.\\n* **Denied topics** - Define a set of topics that\\n are undesirable in the context of your application. The filter will help block them if\\n detected in user queries or model responses.\\n* **Word filters** - Configure filters to help\\n block undesirable words, phrases, and profanity (exact match). Such words can include offensive terms,\\n competitor names, etc.\\n* **Sensitive information filters** - Configure filters to help block or\\n mask sensitive information, such as personally identifiable information (PII), or custom\\n regex in user inputs and model responses. Blocking or masking is done based on probabilistic detection of\\n sensitive information in standard formats in entities such as SSN number, Date of Birth, address, etc. This also allows configuring regular expression based\\n detection of patterns for identifiers.\\n* **Contextual grounding check** - Help detect and filter\\n hallucinations in model responses based on grounding in a source and\\n relevance to the user query.\\n\\nFor more information, see How Amazon Bedrock Guardrails works\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/APIReference/API_CreateGuardrail.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"How do I optimize prompts to achieve deterministic responses on Amazon Bedrock?\",\"context\":\"### Set up guardrails\\n\\nTo control the responses from the FMs, set up guardrails for Amazon Bedrock. You can consistently apply the guardrails across multiple FMs. Use guardrails to [block certain topics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html#guardrails-topic-policies), [filter out harmful or unpredictable content](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html#guardrails-content-filters), remove undesirable words, and hide sensitive information. For more information, see [Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html).\\n\\nYou can also customize blocked messages and\u00a0[use the built-in test window to test your guardrail configurations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-test.html). To get controlled and predictable outputs, connect guardrails directly with the FMs when you generate responses\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/bedrock-prompts-deterministic-responses\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"Designing Trust and Safety into Amazon Bedrock powered applications\",\"context\":\"## AI abuse prevention tools and techniques\\n\\nTo maintain trust in your AI services, preventative action is key, while also efficiently planning and managing development resources. Introduce observability and safety guardrails early in development to support long-term scalability and help identify potential issues before they affect your users. To begin this process, thoroughly scope your AI use case with the following actions: \\n\\n* Understand your user\\n* Anticipate potential misuse scenarios\\n* Define your risk tolerance\\n\\nThis scope guides your development of a precise safety framework that addresses the specific risks of your AI implementation while you maintain expected performance. For this scope, you can use AWS specialized tools designed specifically to monitor and protect Amazon Bedrock applications.\\n\\n### Using CloudWatch to monitor Amazon Bedrock\\n\\n[Amazon CloudWatch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html) provides essential visibility into AI system behavior and performance. When you configure comprehensive logging, you can capture important information across user segments and interaction types, such as the following:\\n\\n* Request volumes\\n* Response latencies\\n* Rejection rates\\n* Content filtering triggers\\n\\nYou can use this information to identify potential abuse patterns or unexpected behaviors before they affect operations. CloudWatch dashboards visualize metrics according to monitoring priorities, and automated alerts provide prompt notification when you exceed thresholds. This infrastructure transforms interaction data into actionable insights and supports continuous safety improvement.\\n\\n**Note:** By default, Amazon Bedrock logging is turned off. You must turn on logging for your application. To configure this, contact your account manager.\\n\\n### Using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to customize safeguards\\n\\n[Amazon Bedrock Guardrails ](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/guardrails/)offers configurable protection mechanisms tailored to specific risk profiles and content policies. You can customize Guardrails to match your application requirements, such as:\\n\\n* Define domain-relevant undesirable topics\\n* Configure appropriate content filtering thresholds\\n* Configure sensitive information detection and redaction parameters aligned with data policies\\n\\nAdditionally, you can configure controls that prioritize accuracy and prevent hallucinations while maintaining creative flexibility based on your application needs. When you thoughtfully configure Guardrails, you can balance performance and safety according to your specific use case requirements and risk factors\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/articles/ARw1wa1iv6S82tgMVrznG4cQ/designing-trust-and-safety-into-amazon-bedrock-powered-applications\"}]}}"}]}], "label": "Running Verify Aws Claim"}

{"id": "b9de17b9-d73f-4765-be25-54b98caa681e", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_34OCYotUUApeSoG18isDYP", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-sensitive-filters.html\",\"content\":\"Table of Contents:\\n- Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters (char 0-19337)\\n  - Configure sensitive information policy for your guardrail (char 10889-19337)\\n      - Using Console (char 11079-15835)\\n      - Using API (char 15836-19337)\\n\\n# Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails helps detect sensitive information, such as personally identifiable information\\n(PII), in input prompts or model responses using sensitive information filters. This filter is a probabilistic machine learning (ML) based solution that is context-dependent\\nand detects sensitive information based on the context within input prompts or model responses. You can configure by selecting from a set of built-in PIIs offered by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails specific to your use case\\nor organization by defining it along with regular expressions (custom regex) that work based on pattern matching to block or mask PII data.\\n\\n**Note:**\\n\\nThis filter evaluates text content only. In tool use (function calling) workloads, it does not evaluate the following, so PII in these fields is neither blocked nor masked:\\n\\n* PII the model generates into tool call arguments (`toolUse.input` in Converse, `tool_use` parameters in InvokeModel). For example, if the model passes a customer's email address to a tool that writes a file, that address is not masked.\\n* PII in tool results your application returns to the model (`toolResult`).\\n* PII in the tool definitions you supply (`toolSpec.description`, `toolSpec.inputSchema`).\\n\\nSensitive information detection works across both natural language and code domains,\\nincluding code syntax, comments, string literals, and hybrid content. This helps\\nidentify PII embedded in code elements such as variable names, hardcoded credentials, or\\ncode documentation.\\n\\nYou can configure the following modes for handling sensitive information that\\nguardrails detects:\\n\\n* **Block** \u2014 Sensitive information filter\\n  policies can block requests or responses that include sensitive information.\\n  Examples of such applications might include general questions and answers\\n  based on public documents. If sensitive information is detected in\\n  the prompt or response, the guardrail blocks all the content and returns a\\n  message that you configure.\\n* **Mask** \u2014 Sensitive information filter\\n  policies can anonymize or redact information from model requests or responses.\\n  For example, guardrails mask PIIs while generating summaries of conversations\\n  between users and customer service agents. If sensitive information is detected\\n  in the model request or response, the guardrail masks it and replaces it with\\n  the PII type (for example, `{NAME}` or `{EMAIL}`).\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails offers the following PIIs to block or anonymize:\\n\\n* **General**\\n\\n  + **ADDRESS**\\n\\n    A physical address, such as \\\"100 Main Street, Anytown, USA\\\" or \\\"Suite\\n    #12, Building 123\\\". An address can include information such as the\\n    street, building, location, city, state, country, county, zip code,\\n    precinct, and neighborhood. Isolated mentions of city, state, country\\n    are not considered as valid addresses.\\n  + **AGE**\\n\\n    An individual's age, including the quantity and unit of time. For\\n    example, in the phrase \\\"I am 40 years old,\\\" Amazon Bedrock Guardrails recognizes \\\"40 years\\\"\\n    as an age.\\n  + **NAME**\\n\\n    An individual's name. This entity type does not include titles, such\\n    as Dr., Mr., Mrs., or Miss. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails does not apply this entity type to\\n    names that are part of organizations or addresses. For example,\\n    guardrails recognizes the \\\"John Doe Organization\\\" as an organization,\\n    and it recognizes \\\"Jane Doe Street\\\" as an address.\\n  + **EMAIL**\\n\\n    An email address, such as\\n    *marymajor@email.com*.\\n  + **PHONE**\\n\\n    A phone number. This entity type also includes fax and pager numbers.\\n  + **USERNAME**\\n\\n    A user name that identifies an account, such as a login name, screen\\n    name, nick name, or handle.\\n  + **PASSWORD**\\n\\n    An alphanumeric string that is used as a password, such as\\n    \\\"**very20special#pass**\\\".\\n  + **DRIVER_ID**\\n\\n    The number assigned to a driver's license, which is an official\\n    document permitting an individual to operate one or more motorized\\n    vehicles on a public road. A driver's license number consists of\\n    alphanumeric characters.\\n  + **LICENSE_PLATE**\\n\\n    A license plate for a vehicle is issued by the state or country where\\n    the vehicle is registered. The format for passenger vehicles is\\n    typically five to eight digits, consisting of upper-case letters and\\n    numbers. The format varies depending on the location of the issuing\\n    state or country.\\n  + **VEHICLE_IDENTIFICATION_NUMBER**\\n\\n    A Vehicle Identification Number (VIN) uniquely identifies a vehicle.\\n    VIN content and format are defined in the *ISO 3779*\\n    specification. Each country has specific codes and formats for VINs.\\n* **Finance**\\n\\n  + **CREDIT_DEBIT_CARD_CVV**\\n\\n    A three-digit card verification code (CVV) that is present on VISA,\\n    MasterCard, and Discover credit and debit cards. For American Express\\n    credit or debit cards, the CVV is a four-digit numeric code.\\n  + **CREDIT_DEBIT_CARD_EXPIRY**\\n\\n    The expiration date for a credit or debit card. This number is usually\\n    four digits long and is often formatted as\\n    *month/year* or *MM/YY*. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails\\n    recognizes expiration dates such as *01/21*,\\n    *01/2021*, and *Jan 2021*.\\n  + **CREDIT_DEBIT_CARD_NUMBER**\\n\\n    The number for a credit or debit card. These numbers can vary from 13\\n    to 16 digits in length. However, Amazon Bedrock also recognizes credit or\\n    debit card numbers when only the last four digits are present.\\n  + **PIN**\\n\\n    A personal identification number (PIN) that could be 4 or 5 digits in\\n    length. As an example, these numbers are used to access bank\\n    accounts.\\n  + **INTERNATIONAL_BANK_ACCOUNT_NUMBER**\\n\\n    An International Bank Account Number has specific formats in each\\n    country.
